---
title: "Companion curriculum"
subtitle: "The teaching modules of the course"
---

The course is built around one exercise, taught on four cases: you reproduce a recorded result, vary the analysis behind it, declare one analysis before you run it, and read your result against those of the class. A short session or a single day has room for that exercise and little else, so the skills around it are taught in these eighteen modules, which run from a first line of R to a reanalysis that you can archive and version. Each module stands on its own, so you can take the one you need and leave the rest.

The modules share the cases between them, and each method is taught on the case that carries it best. The field experiment of the housing-audit case carries random assignment, proportions and binary outcomes, conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, and the simulation of a design. The survey respondents of the immigration-and-trust case carry attitude scales and their reliability, survey weights in a regression on respondents, multilevel models of respondents in countries, and multiple imputation of missing controls. The cohabiting unions of the cohabitation case carry censoring, the life table, the discrete-time models of two competing ways out of a union, and the weights and errors of a survey with a complex design. The country-year panel of the EU-frames case carries a battery of survey items, the weights of averaged cells, panel models and a multiverse of hundreds of specifications. Where a module uses more than one case, it says at the top which sections work on which, and so do the tables below.

Nothing here is required for the short session or for a one-day course, which run in full without any module and with no account to create. Their pages point at some modules as optional preparation, at others as the slower companion of a part of the day, and at the rest as reading for afterwards. The three-day courses and the self-study track are built out of the modules: each day of a three-day course takes the modules that its sessions need, and the self-study track uses every module, each in the stages of the case that carries it. The [last section](#sec-tracks) sets out which formats use which modules.

## Three strands {#sec-strands}

The eighteen modules group into three strands: the computational tools with which an analysis is written, the data management and sharing that let it be built and let others find it and run it again, and the statistical methods with which the cases are analysed. The strands are only a way of reading the curriculum, and you can read across them in whatever order suits you.

## Strand I – Computational tools {#sec-tools}

Three modules on the machinery of an analysis: the language in which it is written, the environment in which it is written, and the document format that holds the code and the prose about it in one file. The R module assumes no programming at all, and its first thirteen sections run their code on the housing-audit data, so that every result on the page can be compared with your own. The IDE module sets Positron, the default IDE of the course, beside RStudio and VS Code. The Quarto module displays its examples without running them, because it is about documents that you render on your own machine.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Getting started with R](intro-r.qmd) | Foundation | What R and an IDE are; the console, the script and the report; objects, vectors and data frames, and why the mean of a 0/1 column is a share; installing and loading packages; reading data and looking at them; the pipe and the datawizard verbs; a share and a difference in shares; a first table, and a first figure with tinyplot and with ggplot2; a first call to `try_spec()`. Then, for a second reading: the Stata file that the original authors deposited, and fetching data from an archive; the three dialects of R; the grammar of graphics in depth; reading a specification curve; naming the estimand with easystats. | Housing audit (sections 1–15 and 18), EU frames (sections 16 and 17) |
| [Positron, RStudio and VS Code](ide.qmd) | Foundation | What an IDE does and what the course needs from one; Positron pane by pane, from the console and the Variables pane to the Data Explorer, Quarto, the Command Palette and Posit Assistant; RStudio and VS Code in brief, with what changes when you move between the three; the browser lab beside the workspace; six steps through a workspace that use every pane that the exercise needs. | Any; the steps use the housing-audit workspace |
| [Quarto and reproducible documents](quarto.qmd) | Foundation | What a `.qmd` file holds and what rendering does to it; the header of the exercise report; the chunk options that the report uses, from `include` and `eval` to `error`; inline code; captions and cross-references; citations drawn from a `.bib` file; projects, folder settings and the freeze cache; publishing a finished document. | Any; the examples come from the housing-audit workspace and this site |

## Strand II – Data management and sharing {#sec-sharing}

Where data come from, how a downloaded survey file becomes the file on which a model is fitted, where finished work is deposited, how all of it is licensed, and how a piece of work is versioned and shared. The four cases reach a researcher by four routes. The housing-audit file is a public download from the Harvard Dataverse, and the cohabitation unions are built from public-use files of the National Survey of Family Growth. The immigration-and-trust data come from the European Social Survey under a free registration, and the Eurobarometer waves of the EU-frames case come from the GESIS archive under terms of use that forbid passing them on. The three-day courses download the raw files of their case on day 1 and build the analysis file from them on day 2, with the first two modules of this strand as their companions. The one-day courses on data tools end with a demonstration of git on the shared screen, and the one-day courses on open science and the three-day courses read the deposits of their case. These four modules take each of those topics further, and they are the ones to read once you have a question of your own to find data for, a survey file of your own to wrangle, or a report of your own to archive.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Social science data sources](data-sources.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | The three routes by which data reach a researcher; a map of the survey programmes, archives and catalogues, household panels and cohorts, official and administrative statistics, international indicators and political datasets, with the access rule for each; the routes of the four cases, from the Harvard Dataverse, the National Center for Health Statistics, the ESS Data Portal and the GESIS archive to the World Bank indicators, the published series and the files of SCORE and Multi100 on the OSF; citing data. | All four (section 3) |
| [Building the analysis file](data-management.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | The steps that every build shares; the analysis file of the immigration-and-trust paper from four rounds of the ESS, with the date of the interview, the vote controls, income and the reversed scales; the first cohabitations and the person-month file of the cohabitation paper, read by column position from the files of the NSFG; the country-year panel of the EU-frames paper from sixteen Eurobarometer waves, with the scales, the three scoring rules, the respondent who named nothing, the averaging into country-years and the macro series; each build checked against the files that the course committed; the habits that carry over to a project of your own. | Immigration and trust (section 2), cohabitation (section 3), EU frames (section 4) |
| [Reproducibility repositories](repositories.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | What a repository has to do; the generalist repositories compared; code forges and why a release needs a DOI; the package of the housing-audit study on the Harvard Dataverse and how a record keeps its versions; the SCORE dossiers of the four papers on the OSF; the Multi100 records; a paper without a deposit of its own; the OSF after 2026; registrations and the preregistration templates behind the block of Task 5; an exercise in finding the record; a route for depositing a reanalysis of your own. | All four (sections 4–8) |
| [Git and GitHub for reproducible research](git-github.qmd) | Advanced | Version control from first principles; git on your own machine; GitHub, remotes, forks, templates and pull requests; what belongs in a repository and what never does, with a public-domain file and licensed survey microdata as the two examples; putting your own reanalysis under version control, one decision per commit. | Housing audit, with the licensed files of the EU-frames case |

## Strand III – Statistical methods {#sec-methods}

Eleven modules on the statistical side of the cases, roughly in the order of the ladder of difficulty: the design of an experiment and the models for a yes-or-no outcome; the causal graph that decides what to compare or hold constant; the survey items, weights and missing answers behind a scale; the event-history models of the cohabitation case; the panel and multilevel models of the EU-frames and immigration-and-trust cases, with their claims at the level of respondents; simulation as a check of a method; and the multiverse, which the class builds in the one-day courses with a methods focus and on day 3 of the three-day courses. Each computes its numbers from the files of the course when the page is built, so a module can be read as a worked analysis as well as an explanation. The participant reading of the EU-frames case, [reading a specification curve](../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd), belongs with this strand without being a module of its own.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Audit experiments](experiments.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | Audit and correspondence studies of discrimination; what random assignment buys, with a check of balance; names as treatments; why a comparison among replies needs care, with a bound on how far a change in who replied could go; randomisation inference; power, and why significant estimates from small studies tend to be too large; the ethics of deceiving the people whom an audit studies. | Housing audit |
| [Binary outcomes](binary-outcomes.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | A 0/1 outcome and its share; the difference in proportions and its standard error; the linear probability model with HC2 standard errors; logistic regression; odds ratios against percentage points and average marginal effects; why a covariate changes an odds ratio even in an experiment. Then an outcome asked once a month: one row per month of a union, the discrete-time logit, a rare outcome, and the linear probability model near zero. Then a survey item in clustered data: logit and probit side by side, errors clustered by country-year, the national unemployment rate between and within countries, an interaction, and a random intercept. | Housing audit (sections 1–7), cohabitation (section 8), EU frames (section 9) |
| [Causal graphs and adjustment sets](dags.qmd) | Intermediate | What a causal graph commits you to; confounders, mediators and colliders; why comparing greetings among replies conditions on a consequence of the name; the graph of the housing-audit case, what counting every delivered email changes, and the adjustment sets of its curve; the graph of the immigration-and-trust case, with votes and verdicts as possible mediators and the coefficient under six sets of controls; selection into cohabitation, the composition of the cohorts and the length of the whole union; graphs written as `dagify()` formulas, a collider in a regression, and the EU-frames graph, whose adjustment set is what two-way fixed effects absorb, with what fixed effects cannot fix and the bailout on the graph; what no statistic computed from the data can settle; your own graph. | Housing audit (sections 1–6), immigration and trust (section 7), cohabitation (section 8), EU frames (section 9) |
| [The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd) | Intermediate | The three items of concern about immigration and their index; the reliability of each scale, and why a single item weakens the coefficient; the rules for unanswered items; the three trust items, why the paper keeps them apart, and what the choice among them does on the curve. Then the instrument behind every outcome of the EU-frames menu: how the framing scales are built from thirteen items and the theory behind the grouping; how the items hang together; exploratory and confirmatory factor structures; reliability; what all of this means for the menu and for the outcome on the curve. | Immigration and trust (section 1), EU frames (section 2) |
| [Weights](weighting.qmd) | Intermediate | The design, post-stratification and population weights of the European Social Survey in a regression on respondents, what each makes the estimate describe, and which of them stay on the curve of the immigration-and-trust case. The weights and the stratified, clustered design of the NSFG, a subpopulation of the survey, and errors that follow the design. Survey weights inside a country-year cell, the effective sample size, precision weights across cells and population weights across countries; why only the population weight changes the estimand; the reproduced coefficient under each weight. | Immigration and trust, cohabitation, EU frames (one section each) |
| [Missing answers](missingness.qmd) | Intermediate | What a respondent who mentions no frame at all does to a share built from mentions; the three mechanisms of missingness, and missing answers at three levels; the rules that the menu offers and what each assumes; multiple imputation against those rules; "don't know" as an answer; the sensitivity of the result to the assumption. Then answers missing on the predictor and on fifteen controls, and the claim of the immigration-and-trust case under multiple imputation. | EU frames, with a section on immigration and trust |
| [Event-history analysis](event-history.qmd) | Intermediate | Time to an event and censoring, and why the share married by the interview mixes the event with the time that each union was observed; the life table, the hazard, and marriage and separation as competing events; person-period data; the discrete-time logit and its baseline of time since the start; the complementary log-log model, the proportional hazards model for time measured in whole months; competing risks with a multinomial logit; period against cohort. | Cohabitation |
| [The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd) | Foundation to advanced | Every model fitted on the EU-frames panel, output by output: why the analysis sits at the country-year level; a first linear model; clustered standard errors; the two fixed-effects designs, and standard errors with few clusters; within and between, with random effects and the within–between model, and the same comparison on the respondents of the immigration-and-trust case; multilevel models; survey weights; Bayesian estimation; bounded outcomes; the results of the five analysts on one scale. | EU frames, with immigration and trust in section 5 |
| [The individual level](individual-level.qmd) | Advanced | Why the level of analysis matters; the respondents of the immigration-and-trust case in country-rounds and countries: the variance at each level, the model of the paper with the degrees of freedom of each level, and composition against context. Then the claim of the EU-frames case where its author fitted it, on a simulated person-level dataset validated against the real respondents: the published model, individual effects against aggregate associations, two designs, levels and evidence, the limits of the simulated data, and the second claim of the paper, on the education gap. | Immigration and trust (sections 2–5), EU frames (sections 6–12) |
| [Simulation as a method](simulation.qmd) | Intermediate | Data with a known recipe: an audit declared and diagnosed with DeclareDesign, recovery of the planted gap across draws, what a comparison among replies does when the name changes who replies, and power by simulation against the analytic curve. Then the simulated person-level data of the EU-frames case: its recipe and its validation, composition against context, a lineup, and a world in which the true effect is zero. | Housing audit (sections 1–4), EU frames (sections 5–7) |
| [The multiverse and its critics](multiverse.qmd) | Intermediate | Where multiverse analysis came from; the three purposes that a multiverse can serve; the debate of 2025–26, read against the small curve of the housing-audit case, on which every specification agrees and a replication still failed; the decomposition of a curve by its decisions; robustness against replicability; the multiverse in teaching. Then the curves of the immigration-and-trust and cohabitation cases, the EU-frames curve of hundreds of specifications with its pruned menu, the estimator as a fork of estimands and the displays of heterogeneity and influence, and the four curves side by side. | Housing audit (sections 1–8), immigration and trust (section 9), cohabitation (section 10), EU frames (section 11), all four (section 12) |

A short session or a one-day course has room for the exercise and a few slides of background, so it uses the modules mainly for preparation and for afterwards. During the day itself, the courses with a methods focus point at the causal-graphs module in Part 2 and at the multiverse module in Part 4, and the EU-frames course points at the statistics module in Part 3 as well. The courses on data tools point at the R and IDE modules in Part 2 and at the Quarto and git modules in Part 4, and the EU-frames course points at the data management module in Part 3. The courses on open science point at the repositories module in Part 4. The three-day courses, on [immigration and trust](../tracks/trust-three-days/index.qmd), [cohabitation](../tracks/cohabitation-three-days/index.qmd) and [EU frames](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/index.qmd), read the data sources, repositories and IDE modules on day 1, when the IDE is installed, the R, Quarto and data management modules on day 2, and the methods modules of their case on day 3, while the [self-study track](../tracks/self-study/index.qmd) uses every module.

## A first route {#sec-route}

If you are new to all of this and want a route through, take the modules in this order, which is also roughly the order of what each one assumes. Sections that work on a case you are not studying can be skipped without losing the thread.

1. **Before the course: [Getting started with R](intro-r.qmd), sections 1 to 13, then [Positron, RStudio and VS Code](ide.qmd).** Arrive able to read a data frame, a pipe and a chain of data verbs, and knowing where the console, the variables and the data viewer are in the IDE that you chose, so that the tasks are about the ideas rather than the syntax.
2. **Before or after the course: [Quarto and reproducible documents](quarto.qmd).** The report that you fill in is a Quarto document, and this module explains every option that it uses.
3. **For the housing-audit case: [Audit experiments](experiments.qmd), sections 1 to 7 of [Binary outcomes](binary-outcomes.qmd), sections 1 to 6 of [Causal graphs and adjustment sets](dags.qmd), and sections 1 to 4 of [Simulation as a method](simulation.qmd).** The design that makes a comparison of randomised groups an estimate of an effect, the models for a yes-or-no outcome, the graph of Task 2 at a slower pace, and what a study of that size can find.
4. **For the immigration-and-trust case: [section 1 of The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd#sec-trust), [the section of Weights on the case](weighting.qmd#sec-trust), [the section on the case in The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd#sec-trust), sections 2 to 5 of [The individual level](individual-level.qmd#sec-trust), and [the section of Missing answers on the case](missingness.qmd#sec-trust).** An attitude scale and its reliability, the weights of a cross-national survey in a regression on respondents, fixed effects against random intercepts, the variance of a claim about individuals at each of its levels, and controls that respondents left unanswered.
5. **For the cohabitation case: [Event-history analysis](event-history.qmd).** Censoring, the life table, person-period data and the discrete-time models of two competing events. The cohabitation sections of the [binary outcomes](binary-outcomes.qmd#sec-cohabitation) and [multiverse](multiverse.qmd#sec-cohabitation) modules come after Task 3 of the case, as those sections say.
6. **For the EU-frames case: [Social science data sources](data-sources.qmd) and section 4 of [Building the analysis file](data-management.qmd#sec-eu-frames), then section 2 of [The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd#sec-eu-frames), [Weights](weighting.qmd#sec-eu-frames), [Missing answers](missingness.qmd) and [The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd).** Where the data come from, the decisions made at the boundary between respondents and cells, and the panel estimators output by output.
7. **After the course: [The multiverse and its critics](multiverse.qmd), and for the EU-frames case sections 6 to 12 of [The individual level](individual-level.qmd#sec-twin) and sections 5 to 7 of [Simulation as a method](simulation.qmd#sec-dgp).** The ideas behind the curve that the class builds and the arguments against them, then the claim at the level of respondents, fitted on simulated data whose recipe is known.
8. **After the course: [Reproducibility repositories](repositories.qmd), then [Git and GitHub](git-github.qmd).** The public records of the cases read as models, and the two modules that turn a report of your own into something archived, versioned and shared.

Read as much or as little as suits you. In a short session or a one-day course the course stands on its own, and the curriculum is there for when you want more, while in the three-day courses and on the self-study track the modules make up much of the course. The [self-study track](../tracks/self-study/index.qmd) follows roughly this route, one case at a time.
